card.hook: Here's a fort that's actually easy to photograph: thick walls about 6 metres high, a gateway, and a wide open approach that lets you step back and fit the lot in one go.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 200 m west of the subject, on the open approach off Rajaji Salai, and face east towards the walls and gateway. It's about 3 minutes on foot from the fort, so walk east and you'll reach it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole frontage in. If you're close and the walls won't fit, drop to 0.5x. Then use zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the gateway arch and wall details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the facade, then slide it a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out and the walls keep their colour.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon. The light is softer and the walls look warmer.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and turn so the fort walls sit over your shoulder. Hold the phone a bit higher and out wide so the walls fit behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Sources disagree on photography inside the fort. Some say parts are off limits and the museum doesn't allow photos, so watch the signs and check when you arrive. It's a working government complex, so you may need photo ID at security.
card.challenge: Get the whole fort in one frame with a strip of open ground in front, then sneak in a close-up of the gateway arch.
card.good_to_know: The English East India Company bought this coastal land in 1639 and finished the fort on 23 April 1644, St George's Day, which is where the name comes from. It was the first English fortress in India, and Chennai grew up around it. Inside stands a 46-metre teakwood flagstaff, one of the tallest in the country.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 200 m west of the subject, on the open approach off Rajaji Salai, and face east towards the walls and gateway. It's about 3 minutes on foot from the fort, so walk east and you'll reach it.

Dwello says <cite index="11-13">the use of flash or tripods might be restricted to protect delicate artifacts.</cite> This is a 'might', not a firm tripod ban.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where a visitor can stand with Fort St. George behind them, or a spot where a passer-by can frame the visitor with the whole fort. The fort pages only describe general photo opportunities (colonial architecture, St. Mary's Church, the Legislative Assembly facade) without naming a place to stand. Napier Bridge is named as a photography favourite, and one page says a photographer shot it from Island Grounds for its reflection on the Coovum, but none of the pages puts the fort behind a visitor there, so I did not list it as a selfie spot. Sources conflict on photography inside the fort: TripXL says <cite index="17-18">photography is permitted in most areas</cite>, while HotelDekho and Viator restrict it. Check on arrival, since the fort houses government offices and rules can change. No page mentions selfie stick rules. Photo ID is needed at entry for security checks, but no page frames this as a safety point.

card.hook: Come evening, Chennai heads to Marina Beach to stroll, fly kites and cool off, and from the top of the lighthouse you can see all of it at once. The beach is about 300 m wide, so there's plenty of open sand and sea to fill your frame.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Chennai Lighthouse observation gallery, near the south end of Marina Beach. The beach spot on the map lies to the north of you, so face north and look along the whole beach.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the beach, sea and skyline in. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched shoreline, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out kites, groups of people or the statues on the promenade.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, tap the brightest part of the sky, then slide it a little darker so the sea and clouds keep their colour.
card.best_time: Some visitors love sunset or evening, while others say morning gives the clearest views. It's busier at weekends and on holidays, so a weekday morning is your quieter option.
card.selfie_here: Head down to the sand near the Chennai Lighthouse at the south end of the beach, because guides name the lighthouse as the backdrop to frame against the sunset. Use your front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the lighthouse over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Swimming is legally prohibited here because of the strong undercurrent, so take your photos from the sand or the promenade and don't wade into the water. The lighthouse gallery is a paid, ticketed lift ride, so check opening hours and fees on the day.
card.challenge: Zoom to 2x and catch a kite against the sky with the shoreline sweeping away beneath it.
card.good_to_know: The promenade was laid out in 1884 by the then governor, Mount Stuart Elphinstone Grant Duff. Statues and memorials were added over the years, including the Triumph of Labour and a Gandhi statue. It's one of the busiest beaches in the country, with around 30,000 visitors on a weekday and about 50,000 at weekends and on holidays.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Chennai Lighthouse observation gallery, near the south end of Marina Beach. The beach spot on the map lies to the north of you, so face north and look along the whole beach.

selfie_research.safety: Marina Beach and Elliot's Beach have strong undercurrents, so stay on the sand for photos and do not wade into the water for shots.
selfie_research.notes: No page I found says where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole Marina Beach in view, so ask_someone_spot is null. The Namma Chennai sign is a separate sculpture on the road, not the beach, and its sources do not say the sea is behind it; the 2021 sources may also be out of date. The lighthouse entry is a sunset backdrop suggestion, not a confirmed selfie point. No page I found gives selfie stick or tripod rules for Marina Beach; the only related item was a general photography note saying personal shoots need no special permission.

card.hook: Here's a nice surprise: a colonial-era museum with six buildings, and you can get the classic facade shot from the pavement without buying a ticket. Just keep an eye on the traffic.
card.stand_here: Stand on Pantheon Road, in front of the main museum frontage, and face the old museum building and its facade. The middle of the complex is a short walk to the north-west of this spot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to see the facade the way your eyes do. If you're close to the frontage, tap zoom 0.5x to fit more of the building in. Zoom 2x or higher (depends on your phone) picks out the details without you stepping into the road.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them so the walls don't lean, then tap the facade and slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer on the stonework.
card.selfie_here: Head for the Museum Gardens, on the lawns in front of the Main Building. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and face away from the red-faced Main Building so it sits over your shoulder. The page recommends early morning or early evening light for soft results.
card.ask_someone: If you go in, stand on the worn stone steps on the north face of the Main Building and ask a passer-by to stand a few metres back across the forecourt, so the whole facade fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography isn't allowed in the Raja Ravi Varma painting halls, and commercial photography isn't permitted. Rules inside can vary, so check the official site before you go. In summer, carry water, because Chennai's midday heat can be intense.
card.challenge: Get the facade with the walls dead straight against the gridlines, then spot one detail in the stonework and zoom in on it.
card.good_to_know: The museum started in 1851, which makes it the second oldest museum in India, and it moved to Pantheon Road in 1854. The complex covers around 16 acres, with six buildings and 46 galleries, and it also holds the Connemara Public Library and the National Art Gallery. Inside the gates, the Museum Theatre is a rare Italianate-style building from the late 19th century, with a high plinth, a tall flight of steps and a verandah of arched columns.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Pantheon Road, in front of the main museum frontage, and face the old museum building and its facade. The middle of the complex is a short walk to the north-west of this spot.

selfie_research.notes: Sources disagree on opening days and hours: one says open Tuesday to Sunday 9:30 to 5, another says closed Fridays 9:30 to 5, and a third says every day 10:30 to 6:30. card.hook: Picture a huge brick-red building with towers against the sky, and a forecourt humming with people in front of it. That's Chennai Central, and the crowd is part of the picture.
card.stand_here: Walk east along Poonamallee High Road towards the station and stop on the forecourt side, opposite the main entrance. Face the station and you'll have the whole front in view, which is the classic postcard angle.
card.zoom: Start at 1x, which should catch most of the front. If the towers get chopped off at the sides, tap 0.5x. For a close-up of the clock tower, try 2x or higher, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so they don't lean, then tap the brick-red wall and slide darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: There's no magic hour we can promise here. Whenever you go, wait for a gap in the traffic and people to get a cleaner foreground.
card.selfie_here: Switch to the front camera, tap 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a little low and out in front. That lets you squeeze the big brick building in over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working station, so keep clear of entrances and passenger routes, stay aware of trains, and pause if the crowd builds up. Casual photos are generally fine, but professional shoots may need permission, so check the station's rules before you go.
card.challenge: Get the clock tower dead centre with a tower evenly on each side, and no bus photobombing it. Good luck!
card.good_to_know: The station opened in 1873 to a design by George Harding. Robert Chisholm later added the clock tower and the caps on the main towers, finishing in 1900. The clock tower is about 136 ft tall, and in 2019 the station was renamed after M. G. Ramachandran and a 100 ft flag mast went up out front.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk east along Poonamallee High Road towards the station and stop on the forecourt side, opposite the main entrance. Face the station and you'll have the whole front in view, which is the classic postcard angle.

selfie_research.safety: Stay aware of trains and avoid blocking train operations or passenger movement while taking photos (per airial.travel's Chennai Central FAQ).
selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a specific selfie spot or a photo position with Chennai Central behind the visitor, so I am not giving one. Sources only describe the building in general terms: airial.travel says the exterior architecture is stunning from various angles, and Focuz Studios calls the station a prominent couple-shoot location without naming a spot. The closest named location is the main entrance, which Wikipedia places on Poonamallee High Road at its junction with Pallavan Salai and Wall Tax Road, but no page calls that a photo spot. A Wanderlog reviewer says the outside is the only place to photograph and that photography is not allowed inside, though that is one review, not an official rule. Airial.travel also says drone photography is prohibited in and around railway stations, but it is not a selfie-stick or tripod rule, so I left it out. The sources are not consistent on photography rules, so check on site. Verify any spot on the ground before adding it to the map.

card.hook: Here's a twist: the best outside shot of Chepauk isn't of the stadium, it's of its glow. Wait until the floodlights come on and it floats above the beach trees like a lit-up spaceship.
card.stand_here: Stand on Marina Beach at the northern end, toward the Gandhi statue area. Face west toward the stadium, and its floodlit glow will rise above the beach trees and the sea.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the beach, the trees and the glow all fit in one frame. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the lights closer, and use 0.5x only if you want lots of foreground.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on night mode, tap the bright lights, then slide the brightness down a little so the floodlights don't turn into a white blur.
card.best_time: Go in the evening, once the floodlights are on. That's when the stadium gets its strong glowing shape.
card.selfie_here: The northern end of Marina Beach is a good dusk backdrop once the lights are on, though it works better as a glow than a sharp stadium. Use the front camera, switch to a wider setting if your phone has one, and keep the glow over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the ground, ordinary cameras are generally allowed but professional gear may need authorisation, so check the stadium rules on the day. On match days, expect crowds and possible closures near Wallajah Road.
card.challenge: Place the glow on one of the upper gridlines, keep the horizon dead straight, and see if you can get the trees along the bottom without any people's heads in the way.
card.good_to_know: Chepauk dates from 1916 and is the second oldest international cricket stadium in India still in use, after Eden Gardens in Kolkata. It hosted its first Test in 1934, and rebuilding has taken the capacity to around 38,000. It's home to the Chennai Super Kings.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Marina Beach at the northern end, toward the Gandhi statue area. Face west toward the stadium, and its floodlit glow will rise above the beach trees and the sea.

selfie_research.notes: The sources I found do not name a spot where a visitor can take a selfie with the stadium directly behind them. The only spot offered is the Marina Beach suggestion, which is a dusk photo of the stadium's lights seen from the beach, so it is a weak fit for a selfie. The Anna Pavilion upper tier and Wadekar Stand upper tier are photo spots from inside the stands and show the pitch, not the stadium from outside, so I left them out. No page names a spot where a passer-by should photograph the visitor with the whole stadium, so ask_someone_spot is null. No page mentions selfie stick or tripod rules, and none gives a safety point. The Justdial listing places the stadium opposite Chepauk Railway Station, but it does not describe a photo position, so I did not use it.
